prompt:
An orthopaedic device company is designing a titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) bone fixation plate for mid-shaft femoral fractures. The plate is a 12-hole narrow dynamic compression plate (DCP) with a thickness of 5.0 mm and width of 16 mm. The plate is designed to bear the full physiological load during the healing period, with a rated load capacity of 4x body weight (corresponding to peak forces during stair climbing for a 90 kg patient: approximately 3530 N).

The biomechanical analysis demonstrates the plate can withstand the cyclic loading of ambulation with a fatigue safety factor of 2.5 over the expected 6-month healing period. The plate stiffness is 280 N/mm in bending, compared to intact femoral cortical bone stiffness of approximately 60 N/mm for an equivalent cross-section. The surgeon's technique guide recommends the plate be left in situ permanently unless the patient requests removal, as routine removal surgery poses its own risks.

Screw fixation uses 4.5 mm cortical screws with bicortical purchase. The minimum screw pullout strength is specified as 800 N based on testing in synthetic bone blocks (Sawbones, 20 PCF density, representing normal cortical bone). The device is CE marked under MDR (EU 2017/745) as a Class IIb implant, with clinical evaluation based on equivalence to predicate devices per MEDDEV 2.7/1 Rev 4.

seeded_faults.description: The plate bending stiffness (280 N/mm) is approximately 4.7 times the stiffness of the equivalent bone cross-section (60 N/mm). This extreme stiffness mismatch causes stress shielding — the plate carries a disproportionate share of mechanical load, depriving the healing bone of the mechanical stimulation required for remodelling per Wolff's Law. The recommendation to leave the plate in situ permanently compounds this: chronic stress shielding leads to cortical bone thinning (osteopenia) under the plate, weakening the bone at the plate-bone interface over years. When (if) the plate is eventually removed — or if it fatigues and fails after many years — the weakened bone is vulnerable to re-fracture. Published clinical evidence (Tonino et al., 1976; Uhthoff & Finnegan, 1983) and modern consensus (AO Foundation principles) demonstrate that plate stiffness should be minimised to the degree consistent with adequate fixation stability, using limited-contact plate designs, titanium (lower modulus than steel), or modern locking plate constructs. The design analysis focuses solely on plate survival and ignores the biological consequence of excessive rigidity.
seeded_faults.location_hint: Plate stiffness of 280 N/mm vs bone stiffness of 60 N/mm, permanent retention recommendation

seeded_faults.description: The minimum screw pullout strength is specified as 800 N based on testing in 20 PCF (0.32 g/cc) synthetic bone, representing normal healthy cortical bone. However, mid-shaft femoral fractures frequently occur in osteoporotic patients (elderly, post-menopausal women), where cortical bone density and screw purchase are substantially reduced. ASTM F1839 specifies synthetic bone test blocks across a density range (5-50 PCF), and ASTM F543 (Standard Specification for Metallic Medical Bone Screws) requires pullout testing in materials representative of the intended clinical population. Testing exclusively in 20 PCF blocks does not characterise performance in osteoporotic bone (typically 10-15 PCF cortical equivalent, where pullout strength drops to 300-500 N). For a plate rated to 4x body weight (3530 N for 90 kg), distributed across screws, individual screw loads during peak activity can reach 400-600 N — potentially exceeding osteoporotic pullout strength. The specification omits any osteoporotic use case or contraindication.
seeded_faults.location_hint: Screw pullout testing in 20 PCF synthetic bone only

ground_truth_notes: Stress shielding and Wolff's Law per Wolff (1892), Uhthoff & Finnegan (1983) JBJS, and Tonino et al. (1976). AO Foundation Principles of Fracture Management (Ruedi, Buckley & Moran, 3rd ed.) discusses stiffness matching and biological fixation. ASTM F543 Standard Specification for Metallic Medical Bone Screws specifies pullout testing requirements. ASTM F1839 covers rigid polyurethane foam test blocks across density ranges. Osteoporotic bone density and screw purchase reduction per Chapman et al. (1996) JAAOS and Seebeck et al. (2004) JBJS. MDR (EU 2017/745) Annex XIV requires clinical evaluation to consider the full intended patient population including foreseeable subgroups.
